questions.prompt: Why does Christensen move to the mechanical excavator industry in Chapter 3?
choices: To replace the disruption theory with a new framework
To test whether the same pattern survives outside disk drives
To prove every industry changes at the same speed

explanation.gentle: The chapter checks whether the disruptive pattern repeats in a very different industry.
explanation.direct: Christensen is stress-testing the theory across industries rather than relying on one famous case.
explanation.competitive: The argument has to win away from home to stay credible.

questions.prompt: What role do cable-actuated excavators play in the chapter's logic?
choices: They show that incumbents were defending a market that still made sense to serve
They prove the old technology had no real customers left
They demonstrate that incumbents never valued performance

explanation.gentle: Cable machines matter because the old market fit was real, not absurd.
explanation.direct: The chapter keeps incumbent behavior grounded by showing that the established product still matched mainstream demand.
explanation.competitive: The old product earned its market, which is why the entrant had to start elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the hydraulic excavator foothold?
choices: A disruptive technology must beat the mainstream product immediately
A product can begin in another market where different tradeoffs make it useful enough to improve
A technology only matters if incumbents have never heard of it

explanation.gentle: The foothold shows that a product can matter first in another market rather than the mainstream one.
explanation.direct: Hydraulics illustrate that early usefulness in an alternate network can be enough to keep learning alive.
explanation.competitive: The first win is not dominance. It is a market where the product gets to breathe.

questions.prompt: Devon's company finally built the smaller product, but it still pitches it only to premium buyers who do not want it. Which response fits Chapter 3?
choices: The company has solved the problem because it now owns the technology
The company should find the market that values the product first instead of forcing the old audience
The company should abandon the product until premium buyers change their minds

explanation.gentle: Owning the product is not enough if the first market for it is still being ignored.
explanation.direct: Chapter 3 separates technology ownership from commercialization fit, which is why the launch audience matters.
explanation.competitive: Building the tool means nothing if the wrong crowd still runs the pitch.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the chapter's harder limit on incumbent response?
choices: Incumbents always lose because they never participate in the new technology
Incumbents can engage the new technology and still stay late if they commercialize it through the old market's standards
Incumbents win automatically once they copy the entrant's design

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that response can still be weak if it is shaped by the wrong market logic.
explanation.direct: Christensen's sharper claim is that engagement with the technology does not guarantee fit with the market that values it first.
explanation.competitive: Touching the disruption is not the same as launching it in the right world.

questions.prompt: What would be a misreading of Chapter 3?
choices: The chapter shows a repeated structure across industries
The chapter proves every industry will repeat the same details in the same order
The chapter strengthens the theory by moving beyond disk drives

explanation.gentle: The chapter supports repeated structure, not a rigid script with copied details in every industry.
explanation.direct: Christensen is arguing for recurrence in mechanism, not identical surface history everywhere.
explanation.competitive: Same trap is not the same timeline.

questions.prompt: A workshop team dismisses a compact design because it looks weak by the advanced competition standard, even though beginners can use it. What should they examine?
choices: Whether the compact design has a first market with different standards
Whether all beginner use should be ignored
Whether the design should be judged only by the highest-status users

explanation.gentle: They should ask whether the design fits a different user group well enough to matter first.
explanation.direct: The chapter turns this into a foothold question rather than a prestige question.
explanation.competitive: A different market may be giving the tool life before the elite standard ever will.

questions.prompt: Why does Elena misjudge the smaller home-repair tool when she compares it only to heavy-duty tasks?
choices: Because the tool has no real market
Because she is ignoring the first use case where the tool actually fits
Because compact tools are always stronger than full-size ones

explanation.gentle: The tool may be weak for one job and still be right for the use case that first makes it worthwhile.
explanation.direct: She is applying the old benchmark instead of asking what first market gives the product real value.
explanation.competitive: She is grading the foothold tool by the crown-jewel task.

questions.prompt: Why is Chapter 3 stronger than a simple "here is another example" move?
choices: Because it proves surface details do not matter at all
Because it shows the same underlying mechanism recurring in a different industry
Because it abandons the value-network idea and replaces it

explanation.gentle: The chapter matters because a repeated mechanism in a different setting strengthens the theory.
explanation.direct: Christensen is using recurrence across industries to argue that the pattern is structural rather than accidental.
explanation.competitive: New machinery, same deeper trap. That is what gives the chapter force.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 3 shows footholds forming in neglected markets, what question naturally pushes into Chapter 4?
choices: Why are incumbents so ready to move upward while leaving those lower-end footholds behind?
Why do entrants always choose construction industries first?
Why should every incumbent copy every entrant immediately?

explanation.gentle: The next issue is the structural pull that makes incumbents keep rising while footholds grow below.
explanation.direct: Chapter 4 follows by asking why upmarket movement is attractive and downmarket defense is so hard to justify.
explanation.competitive: Once the foothold is real, the next question is why the leader keeps clearing space for it.
